6.4 — Boots: Double Jump

The potion raised a number that already had a ceiling. The boots change something else entirely: they change what your level design is allowed to ask for. One pickup that grants a second jump in mid-air rewrites every gap in the cave — including the gaps you have not built yet. Today: a counter, the single moment it goes back up, and a gate with no lock on it.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I make a double jump?”Outline only
Break It Down~10 minOutline only

Tap the key in mid-air and jump a second time — but only while you are carrying the boots. As one problem it is not startable, because the question your jump has been asking since 6.2 ("am I standing on something?") has a false answer in exactly the situation the second jump happens in.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Count the jumps you have leftwhat does this part do?Read: 2.1 — Coins: Triggers, Tags & Your First Stat: the count field you declared in the class body, and the rule that state which has to survive a frame belongs to the object
  2. Spend one at the instant the jump fireswhat does this part do?Read: the "spend rule" you wrote for the coyote window in 6.3 — jump and the window is gone — and the jump line itself in 6.1
  3. Give it back the moment you land, in the one place the ground check already runswhat does this part do?Read: 6.2 — Ground Checks: No Infinite Jumps: the check itself, and the rule from 6.3 that it is computed in exactly one place
  4. Let the jump condition ask about the counterwhat does this part do?Read: the compound condition you wrote in 6.2 and the grace window you added to it in 6.3
  5. Build the pickup that changes the numberwhat does this part do?Read: 2.1 — Coins: Triggers, Tags & Your First Stat (tag, trigger, callback, destroy) and 2.3 — Healing Pickups & the Max-Health Cap (the pickup that moves a ceiling)
  6. Put the boots where the level can ask for themwhat does this part do?Read: the prefab-versus-instance rule and the placement work in 2.1, and the playtest habits from 2.4

Five of those six parts are things you have already built, and the sixth is arithmetic on a number. What is genuinely new is small enough to miss: a jump is now legal in the one situation where the ground check says no, so the ground check stops being the whole answer and becomes one term in a question about *how many*. Choosing the field that matches that question — instead of re-arranging a boolean until it fits — is the whole lesson. The code is four lines; the decision is the work.

The test for a finished split: does the part name something you could point at — a field, a line, a branch, an object in the Hierarchy? "Make a double jump" points at nothing. "Where the counter goes back up" points at one branch of one method, and that is a part.

Connect it to something you already built

Very little in this course is new. Most of it is something you have already done, pointed in a different direction — and saying which one out loud is how you stop relearning it every time.

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

The counter and the maximum are two fields. Which one belongs in the Inspector and which one stays private? Say what a designer can do to your game with each of those two answers.

There is exactly one moment in the whole game where the count should go back up. Name it before you read on — and say what goes wrong the day it gets decided in two places.

In 2.1 the coin was a tag, a trigger, a number that went up and a destroy. Which part above is that same recipe — and what does the number do this time that the coin count never did?

In 2.3 the potion changed a value that already had a ceiling, and the rule that held it there lived inside the method that changed it. Which part above is that potion — and of the two numbers the boots can touch, which is the ceiling and which is the running total?

In 3.3 the turret remembered a moment and compared the clock against it, and in 6.3 you wrote that same comparison twice more for coyote time and the jump buffer. Which part above is that pattern a third time — and is the thing being remembered a moment, or an amount?

In 6.2 the jump condition was a single question, and in 6.3 you made it compound by adding the grace window. Which part above adds the next term — and what is the new question about?

The Problem: One Jump Is Not a Number ~15 min

Your ground check from 6.2 answers one question: may I jump right now? That was enough for one jump. It is not enough for two, because the second jump happens in exactly the situation where the answer is no — you are in the air, the ground check is false, and that is the whole point.

So the boolean is the wrong shape for this problem, and no amount of arranging it will help. Your goal: a character that can jump a second time in mid-air, but only after picking up a pair of boots. Before you write anything, answer these on paper:

QuestionYour answer
What fact does the script need that it does not currently have? Not "am I grounded" — something about how many.
When does that fact go back to its starting value? There is exactly one moment in the whole game where it should reset. Name it.
What is the new jump condition, in English, with an AND in it? Write the sentence before you write the code.
What does the pickup actually change — the maximum, or the remaining count? One of these two makes a bug you will meet in the Bug Hunt. Pick carefully.
A bool says "one", a counter says "how many". A boolean is the right shape for a fact that can only be yes or no — hasAxe in 5.1 was exactly that, because nobody ever needed two axes. A jump allowance is a quantity, and a quantity a designer will want to set to three the week they invent wing boots. Choosing the data type that matches the question is the whole lesson; the code is four lines.

Socratic: Choosing the Data

  1. Where does the jump allowance live — on the player, on the boots, or on a manager? Your answer should sound like the one you gave in 2.1, and for the same reason.
  2. What type is the counter, and what is its starting value in a game with no boots? What does the field default mean to a designer who has never read your code?
  3. Is the reset "when I land" or "when I touch a ground-layer collider"? Are those two statements the same thing in your build?
  4. If the counter resets on landing, what is the counter's value at the moment you walk off a ledge? Is that value a bug waiting to happen?
  5. Should the boots raise the maximum, or refill the remaining count? Describe a game where each is correct.
  6. If your death rule from 2.2 reloads the scene, what happens to a maximum the boots raised — and is that fair, or an accident of where the number lives?
Read the Docs: The API for a Second Jump ~15 min

This is the level-3 substitute for a walkthrough: the API is laid out below and the code is not. You write the file. Between them these rows are the whole job — a field, a subtraction, a condition, a pickup branch, a reset — and every one of them is a call or a declaration you have typed before, in 6.1, 6.2, 6.3 or 2.1. Read the cost column before you pick: a jump you can fire twice can also be fired forever.

APIWhat you getWhat it costs
[SerializeField] private int A class-body field, the declaration form from 1.3 — private to C#, visible in the Inspector, and still there on the next frame. This is the counter, and a second one beside it holds the maximum. The starting value is a design decision, not a formality: the default is what the player gets in a game with no boots, and the Bug Hunt makes you ship the wrong one on purpose. And the type has to match the question — an int cannot say "maybe", a bool cannot say "two left".
jumpsLeft = jumpsLeft - 1; An assignment to a field that already exists — no type in front of the name, the declare-versus-assign rule from 1.3. Write the type in front and you declare a brand-new local that dies at the end of the frame, leaving the real field untouched and the jump unlimited — the exact mistake 2.1 warned about with the coin count.
Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space) True on the single frame the key goes down — the check you chose for the jump in 6.1. GetKey is true on every frame the key is held, so one press becomes a jump every physics step the key is down for. The wrong twin is invisible in the code and obvious in the game.
Rigidbody2D.linearVelocity The body's velocity, and the Unity 6 spelling of it. It is the property 6.1 used to overwrite the vertical half and keep the horizontal — and older tutorials, written for earlier Unity versions, call it something else. Setting the whole vector erases the half you did not mean to touch. And a second jump has one decision in it that a first jump does not: does it replace the vertical velocity, or add to it? Replacing gives the same height every time; adding stacks, so a jump fired while you are still rising goes much higher.
AddForce(Vector2.up * jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse) The other flick from 6.1 — one instant change in momentum, which physics then spends over the following frames. It adds to whatever vertical motion is already there, so the second jump stacks on top of the first without you doing anything to make it. And it divides by mass, so retuning mass silently retunes both jumps.
OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other) and other.CompareTag("Boots") The pickup callback and the tag check you have had since 2.1 — one branch more in a method that already handles the coin and the potion. It fires once per entry, and only if one of the pair carries a trigger collider and one carries a Rigidbody2D. The tag is asked of whichever object owns the collider, and the tag has to exist in the project before the check can ever be true — which is why creating it is the first step below.
other.gameObject and Destroy(Object) The whole object behind the collider you just touched, and the call that removes it at the end of the frame. Plain gameObject is you. Getting the two backwards destroys the player — and Destroy is deferred, so the object is still alive for the rest of the frame.
Debug.Log(object) Prints to the Console — the only feedback this game has. Print the counter and you can watch it fall and refill without any UI existing. Text only, and it prints where you call it. A jump that fires and changes nothing prints nothing unless you print it yourself.
Physics2D.Raycast, Physics2D.OverlapCircle, Collider2D.IsTouchingLayers The ground checks from 6.2, whichever one you chose. Your reset has to listen to that answer and no other. Whatever you chose, the answer is re-derived every frame rather than stored — which is exactly why the refill belongs in the one place it is already computed. A second ground question in your script is a second ground question that can disagree.
Three facts a signature cannot carry. First, the counter is the only new data in this lesson, and everything else is a line you have already written pointed somewhere new — which is why deciding where it goes back up matters more than typing it. Second, the pickup half of this lesson is the recipe in the Unity + C# Quick Reference's Pickup row, unchanged: trigger, CompareTag, change state, Destroy. The boots are a coin whose "change state" is a number rather than a destroy. Third, the bug this lesson produces is not a crash: an unlimited jump, a count that never refills and a maximum the player can raise twice all look like working code and broken play, and the Console stays empty for every one of them.
Read the Docs: Who Owns a Pickup? ~15 min

You built one pickup in 2.3 — the potion — and you put the check on the player. That worked. It is not the only way, and by the time you have five items it is not obviously the best way. Read all three before you build the boots:

ApproachWho notices the overlapWhat it costsWhen it wins
(a) The player's OnTriggerEnter2D with CompareTag The player. It asks "what did I just touch?" and reacts. Every item in the game adds another branch to one file, and every item needs a tag and a collider to exist at all. Now. Two or three items, all doing something to the player. It is the shortest path from idea to playable.
(b) A pickup component on the item itself The item. It checks the Player tag and then changes the player. The item must reach into the player, so it needs a reference — and a wrong tag silently does nothing. When the same pickup behaviour should be reusable on ten objects, and the player file has grown long.
(c) A generic pickup with its effect exposed as an event The item, and the effect is wired in the Inspector rather than in code. The most moving parts, and the hardest to read on your first pass. Also the most reusable. When designers, not programmers, decide what each item does.
Whichever you pick, the item still needs three things. A shape the physics engine can test (a collider, and remember 2.1: two colliders with no body anywhere produce total silence), a way to be identified, and a thing that actually happens when it is collected. Tag, collider, effect. Every pickup all year is those three in a different outfit — and the boots do not change it by a single part.

Pick One and Defend It

  1. Which of the three does your potion use, and which one are you going to use for the boots? If they differ, justify the inconsistency out loud — a partner will ask.
  2. In approach (b), the item changes the player. Where does the item get its reference to the player from — a tag lookup, the collision itself, or an Inspector field?
  3. A pickup with a collider and no Rigidbody2D anywhere in the pair is silent. In the cave, which object in the pair has the body — and does the player still have one after 2.2?
  4. Does the boots item get destroyed on pickup, or switched off? Compare against what you chose for the coin and say whether the reasons are the same.
  5. If you later add a third item — gloves that grant a wall jump — how much of your boots work is copy-paste, and how much is genuinely new?
Build Lab: The Counter ~25 min

There is no code in this section either. The counter is a field, a subtraction and one branch of a method you have already written, and the specification below names the decision to make and stops there.

Architectural specification: the jump allowance.
  • How many fields does this need, and what does each one mean? One of them is a designer's knob and one is nobody else's business — say which is which, and say where each one lives so that a teammate can change the first without opening your script.
  • What is the maximum's default value in a build where the player has no boots? Say it out loud, then check that the field in the Inspector agrees with what you said.
  • Where is the single place the counter resets, and is it nested inside the ground check you already wrote in 6.2? If your reset lives anywhere else, you now own two definitions of "on the ground".
  • What exactly does the new jump condition say? It must contain your ground/coyote logic from 6.3 and a comparison on the counter — write the English sentence first, then translate it.
  • What do you do to the counter at the instant the jump fires? If you skip that, what does the player get for free?
  • Where does the jump impulse itself come from — the same code path for both jumps, or a second one? One path is less code and more bugs of one kind; two paths is more code and more bugs of another. Choose and justify.

Deploy in neutral. Add the counter, wire the reset, and leave the maximum at its default. Play: the character should behave exactly as it did before — one jump, nothing new. If it does not, your counter is wrong and you have not written the pickup yet, which makes the wrong counter much easier to find. Only then change the maximum.

Architectural specification: does the second jump replace or add? Two honest options, and they feel different:
  • Replace the vertical velocity — every jump reaches the same height, whether you fire it at the start of a fall or the top of a rise. Predictable, and it is what most platformers do.
  • Add another impulse — a second jump fired while you are still rising stacks on top of the first and goes much higher. Chaotic, occasionally delightful, and very hard to design levels around.
  • Which one does your 6.1 technique give you by default? Read the two rows of the API table above that cover it rather than guessing. If it is the one you did not want, what is the smallest change that gets you the other, and does it break the first jump?
  • Whichever you choose, the second jump now needs to know which jump it is. Which line of your code already knows?
Build Lab: The Boots and the Soft Gate ~25 min

Step 1 — the tag. There is no Boots tag in this project yet, so make one: Edit → Project Settings → Tags and Layers. While you are in there, read the list of tags that do exist and note how few there are. Tags are cheap but not free — every tag is a name somebody has to remember.

Step 2 — the prefab. Build it the way you built the potion in 2.3. There is no boots sprite anywhere in this project — no prefab, no art, nothing to search for — so pick a sprite you already have and tint it with the Sprite Renderer's Color until it could not be mistaken for a coin. That is greyboxing, and it is what 2.3 did for the potion. Then give it a collider on the root and the tag you just made. Decide whether the collider is a trigger or solid, and be ready to defend the answer — a solid pair of boots you cannot walk over would be a strange item. Put the finished prefab in Assets/Prefabs so the whole game can use it.

Step 3 — place it. The cave scene ships with no Coins, no Spikes and no Turrets. That is not an oversight: it is your level, and it starts empty. Drag a boots instance into the cave and put it somewhere the player has to walk to. Then drag a Coin from Assets/Prefabs in as well — you will need it in the next step.

Architectural specification: the pickup branch.
  • Which callback fires when the player touches the boots — the trigger one or the collision one? The answer depends on the collider setting you chose in Step 2, and it changes the parameter type you are handed.
  • How do you identify the boots from inside that callback, and how do you reach the object that should disappear?
  • What does the branch change on the player — the maximum, or the count? Justify the choice you made on paper earlier, and say what the other one would have felt like to a player who finds a second pair.
  • What do you print so the player can see the change with no UI in the game? The whole project reports through the Console, and it is about to report something worth watching.
  • What happens if you walk into the boots with the counter already at its maximum — a second pair, later in the level? Should that do nothing, or is there a design where it stacks? Who should decide, the code or the designer?

Step 4 — the soft gate. Take the Coin you placed and move it somewhere that is genuinely unreachable with one jump: a high ledge, a shelf across a wide gap. Now the level contains a promise it cannot keep yet — no lock, no door, no damage, just a visible thing you cannot have. Play it with and without the boots, and time how long it takes a tester to work out what the boots are for.

Test the whole loop, including death. Grab the boots, then die on purpose. If your death rule from 2.2 reloads the scene, the Player is rebuilt from the prefab — so where do the boots go, and where does the maximum go? Write down what you observe, decide whether it is the rule you want, and if it is not, say which of the two things has to change: the death rule, or where the boots live.
Bug Hunt: The Infinite Stair ~15 min

Bug Hunt

  1. Set the maximum's default to 2 and never place the boots. Walk the whole cave. What did you just delete from your game, and which single Inspector field was hiding it?
  2. Move the counter's reset out of the ground check and into the top of Update(). Count how many jumps you get in mid-air, and explain why the reset ran while you were falling.
  3. Forget to change the counter when the jump fires. Now walk off a ledge, wait a full three seconds, and press the key. How many jumps did you get, and which line from 6.3 is the missing twin of the line you forgot?
  4. Walk into two boots placed on the same ledge. What is the maximum after the second pair, and what would a player expect to happen?
  5. Grab the boots, then die. If your death rule reloads the scene, is the second jump still available after you respawn? Trace which reload caused the loss, and decide whether the rule is fair.
  6. Make the second jump fire the full-strength impulse instead of matching the first. Jump once, then tap again at the very top of the rise. Describe the motion, and name the technique from 6.1 that produced it.
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Capability Design

  1. Design a third item using the same skeleton — gloves that allow a wall jump, or a hook that pulls you to a ledge. What does the level gain access to? Sell it in two sentences like a designer.
  2. Make the boots required rather than optional: wall off the cave's exit behind a shelf only a double jump reaches. What does a player do when they meet that shelf with no boots — is it frustration or curiosity?
  3. Put a Console line in the pickup that reports the new maximum. What does the player learn from it, and what would they learn if you printed the remaining count instead?
  4. Try giving the boots a permanent effect on the world instead of the player — a platform that only appears after pickup. Which approach from the table of three in this lesson does that need, and why can the player-owned version not do it?
  5. Commit and push: "6.4: double jump + boots + soft gate".

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain why a counter is the right data type here and a bool is not
  • Say exactly where the counter resets, and why there is only one such place
  • Build a pickup end to end — tag, collider, effect — the way you built the potion
  • Say whether your second jump replaces or adds velocity, and defend it
  • Explain what happens to the boots when the player dies, and whether you accept that rule
  • Design a soft gate: visible, unreachable, no damage, no text
  • Break this feature into parts small enough to look each one up on its own, and say in one line what each part does
  • Say which earlier lesson each part of this feature came from, and where you would reread it
  • Commit and push
